deep.reconstruction:
Setting: an inclusion of commutative rings k0 ⊂ K0. A struck-out first version had k0 a domain and K0 its field of fractions, and that is in practice the case needed. Define Ω = {F ∈ K0[T] : F(λ) ∈ k0 for all λ ∈ k0}. In modern language this is Int(k0), the ring of integer-valued polynomials. The previous page is the model case k0 = Z: there Ω = ⊕ Z·C(T,n), the span of the binomial polynomials, presented by generators and multiplication/composition structure constants.

The diagram reads as follows. K0[T] maps to Appl(K0,K0), the set maps K0 → K0. Ω corresponds to maps of pairs (K0,k0) → (K0,k0), i.e. maps that preserve k0.

Claims on the page:
(1) Ω is a k0-subalgebra of K0[T] and is stable under composition F∘G.
(2) Ω acts on k0 by evaluation. This action is compatible with +, scalar multiplication, product and composition, so k0 is a 'module' over the composition structure (an Ω-ring).
(3) One wants F(x+y) = Σ G_i(x)H_i(y) and F(xy) = Σ J_α(x)K_α(y), with Σ G_i⊗H_i and Σ J_α⊗K_α well-defined elements of Ω⊗_{k0}Ω. The margin note says this works ('OK') if Ω is a free k0-module.
(4) Lemma: for M a free k0-module, Ω_M := {F ∈ K0[T]⊗_{K0}M_{K0} : F(x) ∈ M for all x ∈ k0} identifies with Ω⊗_{k0}M.

Application of the lemma. View F(X+Y) =: Δ_a F and F(XY) =: Δ_m F in K0[X,Y] = K0[X]⊗K0[Y]. These are integer-valued on k0², so applying the lemma with M = Ω gives co-addition Δ_a and co-multiplication Δ_m maps Ω → Ω⊗Ω.

Composite consequences recorded at the bottom of the page:
- F∘(P+Q) = Σ (G_i∘P)(H_i∘Q)
- F∘(PQ) = Σ (J_α∘P)(K_α∘Q)
- F∘(λT) = Σ J_α(λ)K_α = Σ K_α(λ)J_α (by symmetry of Δ_m), which gives the k0-linear co-structure.

Taken together: Ω is a k0-biring (a co-ring object in k0-algebras) with a composition product. That makes it a k0-plethory in the sense of Tall–Wraith / Borger–Wieland, and k0 is canonically an Ω-ring. For k0 = Z this is the plethory of numerical polynomials, whose algebras are binomial rings. This page sets up the general framework of what the folder calls 'analyseurs', instantiated on integer-valued polynomials.
errors: The identification Δ_a F, Δ_m F ∈ Ω⊗Ω via the lemma (with M = Ω) also needs Ω⊗_{k0}K0 ≅ K0[T], so that M_{K0} = K0[Y]. This holds when K0 is the fraction field, or a localization, of a domain k0, but not for an arbitrary inclusion k0 ⊂ K0. The struck-out hypothesis is therefore actually needed.

The lemma also uses that k0 → K0 is injective and that M ⊗ K0 has coordinates relative to a basis of M. This is fine for free M, but the statement 'sous-anneau Ω_M' should read sub-module, since M is not a ring.

Freeness of Ω is sufficient, not necessary. Flatness-type conditions, or the identification Int(k0²) = Int(k0)⊗Int(k0), are the real issue, and this can fail for general domains. Grothendieck does not discuss when Ω is free; for k0 = Z it is (binomial basis), and more generally over Dedekind domains Int(D) is projective of countable rank, hence free.

ideas.what: Ring of integer-valued polynomials Ω = Int(k0) ⊂ K0[T], closed under composition, acting on k0
Co-addition and co-multiplication Δ_a, Δ_m: Ω → Ω⊗Ω from F(X+Y), F(XY), together with composition: Int(k0) as a biring/plethory, and k0 as an algebra over it
ideas.modern_name: k0-plethory (Tall–Wraith monoid), biring structure on Int(D)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Tall–Wraith 1970; Bergman–Hausknecht 1996; Borger–Wieland 2005; for Int(D) specifically J. Elliott (binomial rings 2006, and later work on biring/plethory structures on Int(D))

ideas.what: Lemma: integer-valued polynomials with values in a free module M equal Ω⊗M; used to land Δ in Ω⊗Ω
ideas.modern_name: Int(D,M) ≅ Int(D)⊗M for free M; Int(D²) vs Int(D)⊗Int(D)
ideas.usually_credited_to: folklore in the integer-valued polynomial literature (Cahen–Chabert, Elliott)

missed.claim: Around 1982 Grothendieck independently frames integer-valued polynomials as an operator algebra with composition and co-addition/co-multiplication acting on the base ring. In effect this is a plethory, with k0 as a canonical Ω-ring, and the binomial-ring plethory as the model (previous page). Generalizing beyond Z to arbitrary k0 ⊂ K0 anticipates questions later studied by Elliott and in Borger–Wieland's plethystic algebra.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical priority/independence for the plethory viewpoint on Int(D). It also shows the 'analyseurs' project was oriented toward plethystic algebra (operations on rings), a link not recorded in the literature on Grothendieck's late work.

missed.claim: The condition under which Int(k0) carries the biring structure (freeness, or Int(k0²) = Int(k0)⊗Int(k0)) is flagged but not resolved for general k0.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is precisely the question treated much later in the integer-valued polynomial literature; it is of mostly historical interest now.

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics is elementary and now known (the Int(Z) plethory, binomial rings). But seeing Grothendieck in ~1982 set up the plethory/biring structure on Int(D) for general D, under the name 'analyseurs', is an unrecorded independent anticipation of Borger–Wieland/Elliott-style plethystic algebra.
transcription_corrections: The rotated left-margin note reads 'OK si Ω est un k0-module libre' and is attached to the F(x+y), F(xy) questions.
In the lemma, 'sous-anneau' is likely 'sous-module' (or a misreading); Ω_M ⊂ K0[T]⊗_{K0} M_{K0}, with a struck-out phrase about coefficients.
The right side of the diagram reads Ω ⇢ Appl((K0,k0),(K0,k0)), i.e. maps of pairs.
The superscript over 'sous-algèbre' is the insertion 'k0-', giving 'sous-k0-algèbre'.
'Δ_a' and 'Δ_m' are written with a and m under Δ (additive/multiplicative); the second is not 'Δ_m^*'.
